This is game 201 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:

- CLAUDE.md (187,786 bytes)

- games.md (264,523 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Usage: python3 libs.py <<< "board rows 9..1 as 9 lines of X/O/." ; prints groups and liberties
import sys
cols="ABCDEFGHJ"
rows=[l.split() for l in sys.stdin.read().strip().splitlines()]
rows=[r[1:10] if len(r)>9 else r for r in rows]
B={}
for i,r in enumerate(rows):
    for j,c in enumerate(r): B[(j,9-i)]=c
def nb(p):
    x,y=p
    for q in((x+1,y),(x-1,y),(x,y+1),(x,y-1)):
        if q in B: yield q
seen=set()
for p in B:
    if B[p] in"XO" and p not in seen:
        g=[p];libs=set();k=0;seen.add(p)
        while k<len(g):
            for q in nb(g[k]):
                if B[q]=='.':libs.add(q)
                elif B[q]==B[p] and q not in seen: seen.add(q);g.append(q)
            k+=1
        n=lambda s:",".join(sorted(cols[a]+str(b) for a,b in s))
        print(B[p],n(g),"libs:",len(libs),n(libs))
# Usage: python3 count.py <<'EOF' ...board rows 9..1 pasted from the board output... EOF
# Area count of the CURRENT position: stones + empty regions touching only one colour.
# Empty regions touching both colours are printed as "open" (count for nobody yet).
import sys
cols="ABCDEFGHJ"
rows=[l.split() for l in sys.stdin.read().strip().splitlines()]
rows=[r[1:10] if len(r)>9 else r for r in rows]
B={}
for i,r in enumerate(rows):
    for j,c in enumerate(r): B[(j,9-i)]=c
def nb(p):
    x,y=p
    for q in((x+1,y),(x-1,y),(x,y+1),(x,y-1)):
        if q in B: yield q
score={"X":0,"O":0}
for p in B:
    if B[p] in "XO": score[B[p]]+=1
seen=set();open_pts=[]
for p in B:
    if B[p]=='.' and p not in seen:
        g=[p];seen.add(p);k=0;touch=set()
        while k<len(g):
            for q in nb(g[k]):
                if B[q]=='.' and q not in seen: seen.add(q);g.append(q)
                elif B[q] in "XO": touch.add(B[q])
            k+=1
        if len(touch)==1: score[touch.pop()]+=len(g)
        else: open_pts+=g
print("Black",score["X"],"White",score["O"],"+7 komi =",score["O"]+7,"open",len(open_pts))
print("open:",",".join(sorted(cols[a]+str(b) for a,b in open_pts)))

I try the chain starting with E3, then follow through with F4 and F5, tracing liberties: the group ends up with just two liberties (F2), but a ladder down to F2 doesn't resolve cleanly since my own stones also end up short on liberties — this line looks too messy to work.

Then I could capture D3 cleanly with D2, since that leaves it with zero liberties. Trying a different approach instead — a simpler atari from F4 on the right side, leading W to extend with E3, which leaves my D4 and E5 groups at just two liberties each, so I need to trace through those liberty counts carefully before committing.

Reassessing honestly: the real question is W's C3-E4 shape, and W's C5 group has plenty of liberties so there's no weakness there to exploit. I think the atari from E3 follows the principle of ataring toward my strength at G3 — after W plays F4, the W chain gets squeezed between my G3, E5, and E3 stones and has to run via F5 or G4, so hane at F5 looks like the right follow-up.

Chasing this further, the fight keeps running into my stones with no clean capture, so the F4 atari line seems to just drag into a messy running fight rather than a clear kill. Pushing into the D3 exchange, the ataris just trade back and forth without resolving in my favor either.

D4 looks like the real weakness here, so sacrificing it might just be necessary — though then I'm worried my territory shrinks to the right side only, which may be too small. Let me reconsider E3 atari instead, since it also helps defend D4 via the D3 connection, then trace through W's likely F4/F5 responses to see if I can keep sente.

Trying F3 after that leads to a split position where White gets the center, which I don't like, so let me try F5 instead to hold the center and see how White responds with F3 or G4.

Let me check the alternative where White plays G4 instead: following that chain through the sequence, my group at G3 ends up getting pressured and could become weak depending on how White responds at H3 or H4. Trying H4 instead of G5 seems to keep White's liberties lower, at F3 and G5.

This chasing sequence through G5, H5, G6, F6, H6 feels like a ladder where my H4/H5 stones risk getting cut off — too messy. Simpler options like E3 or D3 might be better, or I could consider atari-ing at F4 to pressure the E4 cutting stone directly.

Tracing the exchange further, if I play D3, both sides end up with weak chains fighting for liberties — my D-group versus White's E/F group — and it comes down to a tight liberty race where White's follow-up at F3 keeps the pressure mutual rather than decisive.

I keep running the ladder forward and White's chain eventually gets squeezed into one liberty along the edge, letting me capture, but White could sidestep by ataring my group instead, so this line goes too deep to fully verify. I'll settle on E3 as the atari to resolve my weak D4 group more simply.

Actually the standard crosscut principle is to extend rather than atari — extending D4 to D3 gives me three liberties, but White would likely respond with F5, putting my E5 stone into atari, so I need to weigh that trade carefully.

Trying the atari sequence instead: if I play E3 to atari the E4 stone, White pushes out with F4, but that still leaves my E5 stone vulnerable to a follow-up F5 atari, so I'd need to answer there to keep my shape intact.

Then White's chain is down to two liberties and must run via G4 or F3, and I'm checking both escape routes—G5 and H4 responses—to see whether White can break into the right side. The H4 line seems to let White's group gain breathing room toward J4/H3, which isn't great for me, so I'm weighing whether answering at H4 directly keeps White more contained.

Tracing the ladder further, it looks like White keeps crawling toward the J edge while I chase with each atari, but eventually White's chain runs out of liberties near J4/J5 and gets captured, so the ladder works in my favor.

This whole sequence is pretty speculative since a 16k opponent won't play it perfectly, so I'm leaning toward the simpler E3 atari instead — comparing it against just blocking with F4, since E3 keeps things more straightforward.
